::: {.page-intro}
**Make real code faster, and measure the difference.** In groups of **2–3**,
choose an ENSAI, personal, or open-source project, optimize part of its code,
and evaluate the impact on the whole program.
:::

## The task

1. **Introduce the project** and outline its computation.
2. **Identify bottlenecks** using timings or profiling.
3. **Optimize selected blocks** using techniques from the course:
   compilation, vectorization, parallelism, memory locality, batching, or GPU computing.
4. **Validate the results and measure performance**, both for the optimized
   blocks and for the whole program.

Choose a workload with measurable runtime and verifiable outputs.
**Before starting, get my approval**: bring a brief project description,
a representative input, the output to preserve, initial timings,
and an optimization idea suited to your hardware.

## Deliverables

- A **report of about 8 pages** describing your diagnosis, changes, and results.
- **Runnable code**, with dependencies and instructions to reproduce the comparison.
- A **30-minute presentation, including questions**, with every member speaking.

Project work and presentations take place **outside the nine teaching hours**.
Dates will be announced in class.

## Measurements and grading (indication)

Compare the original and optimized code on the same workload, and check
that their outputs agree within a justified tolerance. Document input size
and type, hardware, worker and BLAS thread counts, warmup, repetitions,
and which costs are included.

Report both block and whole-program timings.
**Your analysis matters more than the size of the speedup**:
a carefully measured and explained slowdown is a valid finding.

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---:|
| Correctness and validation | 25% |
| Measurement quality and reproducibility | 25% |
| Bottleneck diagnosis and justification of changes | 25% |
| Clarity of the report and presentation | 25% |


## Rules

- **Any programming language** is allowed.
- **Optimized libraries** are allowed: explain how they help.
- **Confidential projects** may use representative synthetic inputs.
- **AI assistants** are allowed under the conditions below.

## AI assistants {#ai}

Briefly disclose how you used AI tools, including coding agents.
Identify any AI-generated code, what you reviewed, and how you tested it.
You must be able to explain the code underlying your results during the presentation.
